name: planted
statement: The cued base and Olmo-3.1 RL-Zero-Math differ in per-step math skill, and that difference, not solution length, is the gap: RL sharpened the policy's choice at each token (fork tokens, verification and stopping decisions) uniformly over positions, so the base's next-token distribution does not degrade as its own solution grows and loops and unfinished drift are side effects of weaker per-step choices. Olmo-3.1's RL changed activations equally at every position through a concentrated weight direction, so the gap is the same at short and long solutions and at every token budget, and it reflects problem knowledge and step accuracy.
scope: Olmo-3-1025-7B base (with and without the opening cue) vs Olmo-3.1-7B-RL-Zero-Math and Olmo-3-7B-RL-Zero-Math (3.0), MATH-500 and the 328 harder problems, T 0.6-1.0, caps 4k-32k, weight interpolation base + a*(RL - base). It does not cover the plain (uncued) base's format failures, the Code pair, or pass@k ceilings.

explains.how: The 3.0 RL model, trained without truncation negatives, already has the per-step improvement that 3.1 has, so it should match 3.1 and sit above the cued base; the truncation handling is not what separates the releases.

explains.quote: not masking truncated sequences (they are trained as negatives)
explains.how: Truncated negatives are a minor detail of the training signal; the gap comes from reward on correct steps, which this setting shares with the 3.0 run.

explains.quote: from RL's prefix 48 / 41 / 21; from its own prefix 23 / 16 / 38
explains.how: The base finishes more often from RL's prefix because RL's prefix already holds correct steps the base would not produce; the difference is per-step quality of content, not conditioning on its own long text.

explains.quote: T1 cap hits exceed T2's by 15.2 points in Q4
explains.how: The excess cap hits are spread across quartiles by the uniform per-step gap; Q4 is one of several places where weaker step choices show, with no length-dependent hazard.
On harder problems the base makes more wrong turns per solution, which lengthens solutions and exhausts the budget; the cap hits follow from weaker per-step skill, not from a length deficit.
At T 0.6 loops arise when the base's per-step choices at fork tokens are poor and it re-enters a state it cannot leave; the cause is a step-level weakness, not growing context.

explains.quote: diverge on math solutions, more with depth
explains.how: The RL change shows on math tokens because those are where the improved step choices apply; depth here means more math steps, and the divergence is equal per step.
Non-looping cap hits are base answers that wander because step choices are weak, so they would be fixed by better steps at any position, not by long-context repair.

explains.quote: the gain is more answers finishing under the cap
explains.how: A no-training change lifts MATH-500 through better stopping and verification decisions at each step, which makes answers finish; it is the same per-step mechanism.

conflicts.how: The shortest-solution quartile already has an 11-point gap, exactly as a uniform per-step deficit predicts, since short solutions still contain the weaker steps.

conflicts.quote: finished with a wrong answer on 33
conflicts.how: Most RL-only hard problems are base answers that finished wrong, which is expected when the base makes more per-step errors at any position; no late drift needs to be assumed.
Misreads and slips are per-step errors, which is the mechanism: RL reduced them uniformly.

conflicts.quote: the top 4 % of positions carry 38.7 % of KL
conflicts.how: The theory predicts KL concentrated at a few fork tokens and flat over position; this readout is concentrated by token, which fits, and it does not report position.

rival: The base degrades as its own solution grows, and RL (with truncated rollouts trained as negatives) repaired a long-horizon self-conditioning deficit that appears only deep inside long math contexts. Separation: the rival predicts KL(RL||base) per token on RL's own long answers rises with position, that the gap closes or reverses at a 4k cap, and that Olmo-3.0 RL (no truncation negatives) is well below 3.1 at T 1.0. This theory predicts flat KL over position, RL leading at every cap, and 3.0 about as good as 3.1.

predictions.experiment: Olmo-3-7B-RL-Zero-Math (3.0 release), plain prompt, T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, cap 16,384, grader v3, MATH-500 one sample
predictions.refuted_by: 3.0 scores 400 or fewer, well below 3.1's 463, or has far more cap hits than 3.1

predictions.experiment: Teacher-forced KL(RL||base) per token after the cue on RL's own T 1.0 MATH-500 answers longer than 8,000 tokens; ratio of mean KL in the last quarter of positions to the first quarter
Existing T 1.0 MATH-500 answers of the cued base (410) and RL (463) rescored with every answer truncated at 4,096 generated tokens (an unfinished answer counts wrong); RL minus cued base
predictions.refuted_by: RL trails the cued base at the 4,096 cap

predictions.experiment: Base continues at T 1.0 from the first 40 % of RL's right answer vs from the first 40 % of its own answer, on the base's 77 hard-328 cap-hit problems with the cue; difference in finish rate (no cap hit)
base + 0.5*(RL - base) with the cue, T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, hard 328, grader v3, one sample; cap hits
predictions.refuted_by: cap hits fall to 45 or fewer
